articles.text: Piedmont’s teachers union has begun negotiations over salaries and benefits with new School Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. Before sitting at the bargaining table on September 7, teachers rallied for support from the community at their respective schools. Teachers plan to continue to make their pocketbooks a topic visible to parents and students with rallies in front of schools during student drop off on September 21 and 28 as well. Teachers also plan to rally today, September 13, at 5:45 p.m. at City Hall prior to the School Board meeting. They plan to speak at the meeting which starts at 7:00 p.m. The union, the Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT), has joined the East Bay Coalition for Student Success, a group of 19 teachers unions including Pleasanton, Dublin, San Ramon, Pittsburg and Orinda. “I’d say it’s a pretty conservative estimate to say we’d need something like a 14.5% salary increase just to get us back to the spending power we had this time last year. The cost to give all staff members a 1% raise would be $340,000. articles.text: Five public safety cameras for police surveillance will be installed on September 19, according to the City of Piedmont. The cameras will be placed at strategic intersections to help police maximize their response to crimes. “It’s exciting to be at this point,” said Lisa Douglas, Support Services Commander for the Police Department. “After several delays related to both logistics and the installation of power and fiber, we are ready for install.” The cameras to be installed will be live-feed cameras, taking video at 30 frames per second. The cameras have a range of 150-200 feet and are intended to strengthen the existing network of Automatic License Plate Readers (ALPR) which are already installed at various entry ways in the city. ALPR use their cameras to identify vehicle license plates and quickly alert police when a stolen vehicle or plate enters the city. The new surveillance cameras will provide the police with additional context, including the flow of traffic, and the ability to acquire images of suspects. articles.text: It was great to read the article in the September 6, 2023 Piedmont Post, titled ‘Piedmont now the largest community youth robotics league in U.S.” Piedmont youth receive considerable benefit from embracing the FIRST organization’s robotics programs, FLL, FTC and FRC. With this success comes a responsibility to support the FIRST organization. When our sons Charlie and Henry showed interest in FTC, my wife Helen Potter and I not only supported two FTC teams in Piedmont, we also supported FIRST by working at the FTC regional tournaments. These tournaments are the competitions that teams attend to test their creations and compete with other FTC teams. While teams learn from designing and building a robot to accomplish specific tasks, they really complete the learning process in the competitions. After volunteering at several FTC tournaments in Northern California, we got to know other team mentors and organizers as well as the leadership of the FIRST organization. These relationships developed and helped tremendously in starting the Highlanders 8033 FRC team in Piedmont. These relationships also led FIRST to ask if Piedmont would support an FTC tournament. With the growth in FLL and FTC, there are not enough tournament slots for all the FTC teams to compete in Northern California. While Piedmont is hosting an FLL tournament on November 5, there are no plans for continuing to host an FTC tournament. Having staffed several FTC tournaments, we were apprehensive to take on such an event, but we jumped in feet first and rallied the Piedmont School District, Piedmont Makers as well as many great volunteers from Piedmont. PUSD and Piedmont Makers blocked out the Morrison Gym and provided support moving tables and chairs, setting up wireless microphones and managing the WiFi environment per FIRST requirements One side of the Morrison Gym was used to support the pits for 16 teams to prepare robots to pass inspections and be ready for competition. The other side of the gym supported the competition field and competition management systems, referees, and field technical support as well as the audience. Yes, this was a lot of work and typically covered a two-day period for set up and tear down. FIRST depends on communities like Piedmont to step up and support FTC competitions, especially a community that has the largest youth robotics league in the U.S. It seems a bit disingenuous for six Piedmont FTC teams to take up tournament slots in Northern California without contributing tournament slots for other FTC teams. Piedmont has supported three FTC tournaments, most recently following the COVID shut down in 2022. We urge the Piedmont robotics community to continue to host FTC tournaments for as long as FTC teams exist here. There is an established knowledge base; lessons have been learned, tournament operations have been documented for the Morrison gym. articles.text: One of my favorite biblical scenes comes at the end of the Book of Genesis. Here, the Joseph saga draws to its dramatic finish. In Egypt where Joseph, sold into slavery by his brothers, has risen to become second in command to the King of Egypt; where Joseph has used his vast power to save his family, and apparently much of ancient Middle East, from famine by storing great quantities of grain during seven years of abundant harvest; where Joseph has revealed his identity to his brothers who did not initially recognize him; the patriarch Jacob, the father of Joseph and his eleven brothers dies. The brothers tremble in fear believing that with the death of their father Joseph will now turn on them in vengeful wrath. In the face of their trembling Joseph speaks, “You meant to do me evil. God used your evil for good, saving many human lives from starvation in the process.” The theology behind Joseph’s words is profound. While God does not cause evil, pain and suffering, God can use these, indeed, transform these in order to bring about good. Chaos, terror and grave inhumanity litter the landscape of human history. It is the work of God to see all the brokenness, to gently gather it up and, out of the rubble, fashion faith, hope and love. articles.text: Meetings to be held at both City Hall and Community Hall The City of Piedmont and the Police Department have organized three upcoming meetings for community members to voice their concerns surrounding crime and public safety in the city. Monday, September 18, 6 pm City Council meeting Quarterly Crime Report to City Council Chief of Police Jeremy Bowers will present the quarterly crime report to City Council with a description of crime statistics through June 30. At the meeting, Police Chief Bowers will provide another presentation on crime data and police strategies as well as share his insight from the September 27th town hall meeting. Following public comments, the Public Safety Committee will hold a discussion of the presentation. Community members are encouraged to attend one or all of the upcoming meetings.

articles.text: The Piedmont Unified School District has confirmed that a public meeting regarding the Witter Field project will be held on Tuesday, September 26, in the Wildwood School auditorium at 6 p.m. The meeting will give residents the chance to discuss the progress on the project and receive an updated Witter Field irrigation and drainage plan. Director of Facilities Pete Palmer will lead the discussion. Also attending the meeting will be Devin Conway of Verde Design Civil Engineers, Daniel Gonzales the City of Piedmont Public Works Director, and School Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. For a number of months neighbors have raised questions about possible flooding in neighborhoods below the field, and drainage calculations have been questioned. The school district has reduced the peak flow rate for the Witter Field area by approximately 20% at the request of the City. “PUSD reduced the storm water flow into the City storm drain system by reducing the size of the inlet pipe diameter [to slow the flow rate],” explained Palmer. At this time Bothman Construction is still planning on completing all work and reopening the field no later than December 1 despite a delay by EBMUD. Parking restrictions on Palm Drive will also be a topic of discussion at the meeting. Updates on the construction project are posted at Piedmont. k12.ca.us/ref/facilities/witter-field-renovation For more information, contact Pete Palmer at ppalmer@piedmont.k12ca.us or call 594-2877. articles.text: Meeting for new parents scheduled for September 19 The Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) has announced that Kim Hunter and Catie Osborn will co-chair this year’s Giving Campaign. Hunter is the parent of kids at Piedmont Middle and Piedmont High Schools, and Osborn, who grew up in Piedmont, has two at Havens. “I was in Chicago and came back to the Bay Area to be close to my family. We chose Piedmont so our kids could get the same foundational education that helped me,” she said. Hunter has a specific memory. “We were living in Oakland and drove through Piedmont one day and saw all these enchanting scarecrows. I thought this was an incredibly creative place. We moved here when my boys were still toddlers, and we were thrilled to find a community that truly embraced us.” Both Hunter and Osborn joined the Giving Campaign this year because they know “it’s for the schools. There’s no question that our kids are getting a good education and that they’re enjoying learning,” said Osborn. “They understand the reciprocal relationship between the schools and the city.: “The schools are the heart of the community, and the community supports the schools,” added Hunter. PEF and the Giving Campaign committee invite the community to celebrate the launch of this year’s campaign with a popsicle party at Piedmont Park on Tuesday, September 19, from 3-4 p.m. at Beach School. Popsicles will be donated by Mulberry’s Market. Parents new to Piedmont schools are invited to a reception that evening at 7 p.m. at the Community Hall to learn more. articles.text: Parenting requires a creative mindset. Every day is a new opportunity to solve a problem, learn something new about yourself or your kids and develop a new way of doing things in your routines. All of these things are creative acts. Sometimes creativity is critical for just getting through the stresses in life – like when it’s time to get to the airport and your kids are having meltdowns and you have to figure out how to get everyone out the door. Other times the creative path can help you make the most of the experience of just every day small routines. There are so many benefits to you and your family by following the Creative Path. Here are four that you can focus on: Presence, Process, Potential and Enjoyment. Presence: Be here, in the right now. Not in the future, not in the past. The Creative Path asks you to be completely present. And when it comes to kids, there is nothing more important than being with them in whatever state of mind they are experiencing. It’s so easy when someone is having a tantrum or telling you a detail about their favorite game that you truly don’t care about, to distract ourselves with our phones or work emails. But the Creative Path says, what is here for me to notice and learn if I am fully present? Process: Allow the journey itself to be the destination. It’s not about an end goal. In parenting, we can think every day about what college will my kid attend or what they will do for a career, but, in the end, we have no control over those outcomes. What we do have control over is the process of getting there. Every day are we seeing what our children are passionate about. Are we engaging with our children on what they are learning and loving in life? The Creative Path is about the path, not the destination. Enjoy it. Potential: Live in the excitement of “what if” because if you can dream it, you can create it. On the Creative Path, we can truly become our own wizards and magicians. We can dream and vision and work to create, knowing that it might not end up exactly as we think it might, but also realizing that every moment and every situation has the potential to be exciting and interesting. pages.text: 8 Wednesday, September 13, 2023 Thinking Outside the Classroom Family benefits of following the creative path By Nina Meehan Parenting requires a creative mindset. Every day is a new opportunity to solve a problem, learn something new about yourself or your kids and develop a new way of doing things in your routines. All of these things are creative acts. Sometimes creativity is critical for just getting through the stresses in life – like when it’s time to get to the airport and your kids are having meltdowns and you have to figure out how to get everyone out the door. Other times the creative path can help you make the most of the experience of just every day small routines. There are so many benefits to you and your family by following the Creative Path. Here are four that you can focus on: Presence, Process, Potential and Enjoyment. Presence: Be here, in the right now. Not in the future, not in the past. The Creative Path asks you to be completely present. And when it comes to kids, there is nothing more important than being with them in whatever state of mind they are experiencing. It’s so easy when someone is having a tantrum or telling you a detail about their favorite game that you truly don’t care about, to distract ourselves with our phones or work emails. But the Creative Path says, what is here for me to notice and learn if I am fully present? Process: Allow the journey itself to be the destination. It’s not about an end goal. In parenting, we can think every day about what college will my kid attend or what they will do for a career, but, in the end, we have no control over those outcomes. What we do have control over is the process of getting there. Every day are we seeing what our children are passionate about. Are we engaging with our children on what they are learning and loving in life? The Creative Path is about the path, not the destination. Enjoy it. Potential: Live in the excitement of “what if” because if you can dream it, you can create it. On the Creative Path, we can truly become our own wizards and magicians. We can dream and vision and work to create, knowing that it might not end up exactly as we think it might, but also realizing that every moment and every situation has the potential to be exciting and interesting. What is the opportunity to welcome more music into your life? How can we become the best bread baker in the neighborhood? Is there a new dance move that we all want to learn together? All of these can become amazing “what ifs” if you welcome them. Enjoyment: It’s fun! And we all need fun in our lives. Creativity is fun. It allows for laughter and joy. The slog of life can be super hard. Don’t we deserve some light-hearted enjoyment? The Creative Path can give you that fun because it can be about what feels good. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. The loss to Lick showed some of the same characteristics to Piedmont’s recent 3-0 loss at Skyline, where the Highlanders showed moments of offensive power and defensive stability, but with inconsistent execution. “We’re trying to figure out who fits where. articles.text: Girls team finishes 3rd; Schulte-Sasse 9th of 124 Piedmont’s cross country team traveled to Hidden Valley Park in Martinez for the Ed Sias Invitational last for the start of the season. The Highlanders’ girls’ team ran to a third-place finish out of 16 schools in the small-school category, while the boys’ were eighth of 18. “We have a very young team this year, and it was exciting to see so many of our new runners off to a great start. It was a two-mile course in distance and included two fairly challenging hill climbs – one at the beginning of the race and another right at the end,” said first year head coach Steve Zirkelbach. Leading the girls’ team was sophomore Skylar Best, placing 19th of 119 runners with a time of 13:34.9, while close behind in 23rd was freshman Cora Brozowski Schrader, clocking 13:57. “Cora was really impressive in her high school debut. Skylar Best was the third fastest sophomore in her race and Cora was the fifth fastest freshman,” said Zirkelbach. Rounding out Piedmont’s top five were senior Jamie Schwarz in 26th with a time of 14:02.2, sophomore Cora Chun in 36th in 14:27.6, and sophomore Quincy Antaya 44th in 14:40.1. “To come in third as a team in a field featuring some very strong NCS contenders like Maria Carrillo, Campolindo, and Carondalet, is very exciting,” Piedmont girls’ team finished 3rd of 16 schools. articles.text: San Francisco Opera’s production of Il Trovatore is playing onstage now through October 1. The opera in four acts by Giuseppe Verdi is set to an Italian libretto written by Salvadore Cammarano and based on the play El trovador by Antonio García Gutiérrez. The play opens with a mother being burned at the stake for suspected witchcraft. She is avenged by her daughter who throws the child of the executioner into the fire. The daughter’s father seeks vengeance for the act and forces his surviving son to devote his life to avenging his brother’s death. Soprano Angel Blue sings the lead role of Leonora, who finds herself in the middle of this cross-generational family feud. The Verdi classic is a story of witchcraft, murder, vengeance and family relationships. articles.text: Pianist Tom Borrow will perform a concert at UC Berkeley’s Hertz Hall, hosted by Cal Performances, on Sunday afternoon, October 1. The 23-year old is a protégé of Murray Perahia, a world renowned pianist and the first North American pianist to win the Leeds International Piano Competition in 1972. Borrow has won every national piano competition in Israel, his native country, where he was part of the Jerusalem Music Centre’s Outstanding Young Musicians program. Bor row’s program will include Debussy’s Images, Book 1, Chopin’s Etudes Nos. 1, 6, 10-12 from Op. 25, Rachmaninoff’s Preludes No. 2, 4 and 5 from Op. 23 and Prelude No. 10. The highlight of his UC Berkeley debut recital is Prokofiev’s Piano Sonata No. 6 in A major, Op. 82, the first of the composer’s “War Sonatas.” “I’m thrilled and excited to come to Cal Performances, an institution with an incredible international reputation,” Borrows said. “I wanted to offer a program worthy of the occasion. It’s challenging for the pianist but also a real and profound journey for me and for the audience.” To purchase tickets and learn more, visit https://calperformances.org/events/2023-24/ recital/tom-borrow-piano. The concert begins at 3 p.m. Photo by Tal Givony Pianist Tom Borrow will appear at Hertz Hall on October 1 in a concert sponsored by Cal Performances.

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s production of POTUS: Or, Behind Every Great Dumbass are Seven Women Trying to Keep Him Alive, premieres this Saturday, September 16. The comedic take on White House events is a feminist-focused satire, premiering just in time for presidential primaries. Playwright Selina Fillinger’s newest play, POTUS, premieres on Saturday, September 16, at Berkeley Repertory Theater. When the president unknowingly spins a public relations nightmare into a global crisis, seven brilliant but beleaguered women must risk it all to keep the commander-in-chief out of trouble. The play features Harriet Deirdre Lovejoy as chief of staff, Kim Blanck as press secretary, Susan Lynskey as secretary, Stephanie Pope Lofgren as the first lady, Dominique Toney as a journalist, Stephanie Styles as the president’s dalliance and Allison Guinn as his sister. POTUS is written by Selina Fillinger and directed by Annie Tippe. Post-show discussions are held on September 29, October 5 and October 10, guided by members of Berkeley Rep’s artistic team. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/ shows/potus/.

articles.text: BroadwaySF welcomes conservationist icon Jane Goodall in discussion at the Golden Gate Theatre on Friday, September 15. For one night only, world-renowned ethologist, conservationist and activist Jane Goodall will be on stage to discuss her decades of work in conservation and as a pioneer in the study of chimpanzees. She began her landmark studies in Africa in 1960 and her research continues to influence scientists and environmentalists today. Goodall is an iconic activist in conservation. The Jane Goodall Institute, which she founded in 1977, is widely recognized for creating innovative conservation and development programs in Africa. Goodall’s global Roots and Shoots program also supports tens of thousands of young people in nearly 100 countries with projects that help environment preservation and animals. As a U.N. Messenger of Peace since 2002, she continues to help the United Nations focus attention on environmental issues, primarily world wildlife and their habitat. Goodall will answer audience questions at the conclusion of her talk. Tickets are available online at: https://www.broadwaysf. com/events/jane-goodall/golden-gate-theatre/calendar/.

articles.text: Marin Theatre Company’s (MTC) adaptation of Homer’s ancient poem Odyssey is playing onstage now through September 24. Writer and director Lisa Peterson’s adaptation of Odyssey is based on Emily Wilson’s 2018 translation of the ancient poem, the first English translation published by a woman. The world premiere of the play opens MTC’s new season. The play features Layla Khoshnoudi, Zamo Mlengana, Anya Whelan-Smith and Sophie Zmorrod, and is set in a present-day relocation center for refugees on the Isle of Lesbos. The four young women are fleeing war and conflict in their home countries and await the next step of their journey on the Isle. They take turns reading and reenacting the ancient epic The Odyssey, finding that it intertwines with their own personal journeys. Layla Khoshnoudi, Zamo Mlengana, Anya Whelan-Smith and Sophie Zmorrod in Marin Theatre Company’s current production of Odyssey Tunsian refugee Anoud, played by Khoshnoudi, is the ‘ringleader’ of the four; Rwandan refugee Zee is played by Mlegngana; Whelan-Smith is Hana from Albania; and Zmorrod plays Syrian refugee Béa. The music and lyrics are by Masi Asare. To purchase tickets and learn more, visit https://www.marintheatre.org/productions/odyssey. Show times are 7:30 p.m. on Wednesdays through Saturdays; and 2 p.m. on weekends. Marin Theatre Company, 397 Miller Avenue, Mill Valley, Phone: (415) 388-5200

Second childhood and all that jazz Saturday night at the PCA Back home in Piedmont on Saturday night, we were treated to a concert at the Center for the Arts with a jazz ensemble with singer Jamie Davis and a quintet of superb jazz musicians. Even though I am not a jazz musician, I appreciate the many aspects of this musical art. My high school music teacher, Samuel R, Browne, was one of the most important jazz pianists of his era. I always like to arrive at the Piedmont Center for the Arts early when the performers are often engaged in a warm- up. Pianist Glenn Pearson seated himself at the piano and began to play. I said to myself: “Pearson sounds a lot like Count Basie.” When Pearson finished his warm-up, all of the musicians began to converse. Wouldn’t you know it… Pearson was directly inspired by Count Basie. All the other musicians are stars in their own right: John Wiitala played bass, Leon Royce Jr. was the very elegant drummer, and Michael O’Neill played saxophone. The featured singer was mellow-voiced Jamie Davis. I think that he brought everyone together. For me, the show was a beautiful look into the past. The first thing I noticed was that every one of the musicians was elegantly dressed, and their demeanor was distinctly professional. Everything seemed to be improvised, but that is the nature of jazz. But these musicians play so well together, you might think that they rehearse on a regular basis. This type of artistry is inspiring. As Davis took the microphone, he introduced each song. He knows exactly how much to talk and exactly what to say. (Oh, how I wish other people would learn this.) Needless to say, the audience loved it all. I have one suggestion only. The Piedmont Center for the Arts has very “live” acoustics. Artificial amplification is never needed. articles.text: It was Jules Feiffer who wrote, “Maturity is a phase. Adolescence is forever.” Indeed. What is there about being an adolescent that leaves such a profound imprint that the memories seem to last a lifetime? Is it that life is lived so intensely, involving a degree of engagement unlike anything that comes before or after? For some, it is only reluctantly left behind, the struggles never completely resolved, and even distorted by time, never forgotten. The film Eighth Grade, written and directed by Bo Burnham, captures perfectly that moment when newbie teen, 13-year-old Kayla (Elsie Fisher), in her last week of middle school, finds herself coping with riptides of emotions, her teen life awash with contradictions that can push her to the edge of panic and desperation while she grasps for control. All the while she creates a façade behind which she can hide what she is actually feeling. This is a remarkable film. But know that it’s not a documentary. It is regrettable that it included material that, while honest, earned it an R rating. Eighth Grade is a fictional narrative that is so steeped in truth it’s painful to watch. It possesses an honesty so stark as to be discomforting. That is how good it is. To be 13 is to live with an abiding sense of anxiety and uncertainty, feelings colliding with the need for affirmation, for acceptance, all of which, in the aggregate, are achingly elusive. As Kayla demonstrates in scene after scene (the film is a series of vignettes of her days in class and at home), to be a tweenteen is to experience change, both physically and emotionally. So direct and yet nuanced is this film, so authentic and even quietly harrowing, that the emotions Kayla experiences permeate every frame and are transferred to the audience. Her interactions can seem both conflicted and comical. In one scene, Kayla’s dad, Mark (Josh Hamilton), is driving her to the mall to meet some kids. Nose in her phone, pauses and glances over at her dad and rolls her eyes, saying to him, “Do you have to stare straight ahead like that?” Mark, ever resilient, but a bit of a helicopter parent, wanting above all to make contact with his daughter, patiently answers, “I’m just staring at the road ahead.” Kayla responds, saying, “Well, can you do it another way?” Supremely contraindicated, Kayla posts installments on YouTube wherein she takes on the persona of a life coach, giving advice to anyone out there in the social media ether who might be listening. In one post, looking directly into the computer’s camera, she says, “A big part of confidence is being brave, and you can’t be brave without being scared.” In truth, she understands in spades the scared part (she’s voted the quietest girl in her class, her default setting). What is aspirational for Kayla is the brave part, as she conducts her youthful quest for that geography known as “cool” and “popular.” The contradiction is that her desire to be “fun” is in conflict with her wish to be, at times, anonymous – to just disappear, such as when she’s invited to a popular girl’s house for a pool-birthday party. Her mantra is “Be brave,” yet while standing behind a glass sliding door, dressed in a swimsuit, looking out at a patio-pool filled with kids, she wishes she were anywhere else. What is at the center of Eighth Grade is Kayla’s abiding self-consciousness. She so much wants a social life, a best friend, a boyfriend; yet, feeling the absence of even one kindred spirit she retreats to social media, her only refuge. In the words of coach Kayla, “Life is putting yourself out there – but where is ‘there’?” What she doesn’t realize is that her peers are also clueless about the whereabouts of “there,” no matter how confident they may appear. Eighth Grade. Directed by Bo Burnham. Starring Elsie Fisher, Daniel Zolghadin, Imani Lewis. 1 hr., 33 min. Rated R. Released 2018. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/MAX/Apple tv. articles.text: Film review By Chris Honoré Before discussing writer/ director Sam Mendes’ film 1917, I would be remiss not to mention Peter Jackson’s extraordinary movie, They Will Not Grow Old. He was given access to hundreds of archival World War I news footage from Britain’s Imperial War Museum – scratched, grainy, and hand cranked film that using state-of-the-art restorative technology, he not only colorized but brought back to life. It’s as if he opened a portal in time. We see young Brits gathered on a battlefield, waiting, some staring into the camera, smiling, their youthful faces filled with an optimistic eagerness that would soon be devastatingly transformed. World War I, which began in July 1914 and lasted until November 1918, was one of the deadliest wars in history. Nine million combatants and seven million civilians were killed as a direct result. Indirectly, 50 to 100 million deaths occurred worldwide, attributed to what was referred to as the “Spanish Flu,” the pandemic thought to have begun in the damp, muddy, disease-ridden trenches on the battlefields, conditions that were almost as lethal as the withering machine gun fire, shelling and chlorine gas faced by the troops. WWI was an extraordinary display of nationalistic hubris, bordering on a collective insanity in which millions of men, on all sides, were sacrificed for mere yards of soil. It was a nightmare of the awful, a killing field of stasis that continued beyond all reason. This is the context for Mendes’ most remarkable film, 1917, set in northern France, at the height of the war. The story is deceptively simple: two young soldiers – Lance Corporal Schofield (George McKay) and Lance Corporal Blake (Dean Charles Chapman) – are ordered by their general to deliver a letter to a command post some eight miles away, instructing the commanding officer for his troops of two battalions, numbering 1,600 to stand down. They are told that all lines of communication have been cut. The intelligence in the letter explains that the Germans have fashioned a trap and should the dawn assault take place, casualties will be grave. The caveat is that to arrive at the command post, the distance to be crossed is a No Man’s Land, comprised of German troops thought to have retreated, desiccated terrain and trenches. The general adds that among the battalions waiting is Corporal Blake’s brother. And so, the two climb up a ladder onto the lip of a deep trench, urging one another on, Schofield expressing his reluctance, yet both feeling the urgency of their mission. What they leave behind are green fields and wildflowers; it’s a beautiful spring afternoon in April. But what they find as they move ever deeper into enemy territory is a landscape of utter destruction – deep craters filled with water and bodies, dead horses, stretching barbed wire, and a horror of mud, death and unrecognizable carrion covered with flies and feeding birds. It is a visit to Hell. Their sense of urgency is palpable; to fail would be catastrophic; they must survive in order to deliver the letter carried inside Corporal Blake’s tunic. Any hint of exposition – backstory, shared memories of origin or tales of home – is inconsequential. What we hear are the sounds of their breathing, the rasp and clank of their gear as Blake and Schofield crouch forward, rifles with bayonets ever at the ready. This is the narrative arc. However, what writer/director Mendes and legendary cinematographer Roger Deakins do is create the illusion that the camera is the third person on the journey and the entire film is shot in one long take, never cutting away. That is not the case, but the impact of this most effective photographic technique is not a conceit and is striking. In other words, 1917 is a truly visual film. It is the camera that propels it forward, Blake and Schofield moving constantly, the story revealed as they grimly survey all that is before them. The question posed is can Mendes and Deakins capture and then sustain the attention of the audience as the fraught images escalate, the faces of the two made grimly fearful by what they witness, leaving them to wonder what, among all this carnage, awaits them. I would suggest that 1917 is an engaging, photographic marvel and an extraordinary achievement. In addition, the film possesses a wonderful score by Thomas Newman and truly fine performances by both MacKay and Chapman. 1917. Directed by Sam Mendes. Starring Dean-Charles Chapman, George MacKay, Daniel Mays, Colin Firth. I hr., 59 min. Rated R. Released in 2019. Nominated for Academy Award as Best Feature movie.

The general adds that among the battalions waiting is Corporal Blake’s brother. And so, the two climb up a ladder onto the lip of a deep trench, urging one another on, Schofield expressing his reluctance, yet both feeling the urgency of their mission. What they leave behind are green fields and wildflowers; it’s a beautiful spring afternoon in April. But what they find as they move ever deeper into enemy territory is a landscape of utter destruction – deep craters filled with water and bodies, dead horses, stretching barbed wire, and a horror of mud, death and unrecognizable carrion covered with flies and feeding birds. It is a visit to Hell. Their sense of urgency is palpable; to fail would be catastrophic; they must survive in order to deliver the letter carried inside Corporal Blake’s tunic. Any hint of exposition – backstory, shared memories of origin or tales of home – is inconsequential. What we hear are the sounds of their breathing, the rasp and clank of their gear as Blake and Schofield crouch forward, rifles with bayonets ever at the ready. This is the narrative arc. However, what writer/director Mendes and legendary cinematographer Roger Deakins do is create the illusion that the camera is the third person on the journey and the entire film is shot in one long take, never cutting away. That is not the case, but the impact of this most effective photographic technique is not a conceit and is striking. In other words, 1917 is a truly visual film. It is the camera that propels it forward, Blake and Schofield moving constantly, the story revealed as they grimly survey all that is before them. The question posed is can Mendes and Deakins capture and then sustain the attention of the audience as the fraught images escalate, the faces of the two made grimly fearful by what they witness, leaving them to wonder what, among all this carnage, awaits them. I would suggest that 1917 is an engaging, photographic marvel and an extraordinary achievement. In addition, the film possesses a wonderful score by Thomas Newman and truly fine performances by both MacKay and Chapman. 1917. Directed by Sam Mendes. MOVIES FOR KIDS Eighth Grade a marvel of a film about teens By Chris Honoré It was Jules Feiffer who wrote, “Maturity is a phase. Adolescence is forever.” Indeed. What is there about being an adolescent that leaves such a profound imprint that the memories seem to last a lifetime? Is it that life is lived so intensely, involving a degree of engagement unlike anything that comes before or after? For some, it is only reluctantly left behind, the struggles never completely resolved, and even distorted by time, never forgotten. The film Eighth Grade, written and directed by Bo Burnham, captures perfectly that moment when newbie teen, 13-year-old Kayla (Elsie Fisher), in her last week of middle school, finds herself coping with riptides of emotions, her teen life awash with contradictions that can push her to the edge of panic and desperation while she grasps for control. All the while she creates a façade behind which she can hide what she is actually feeling. This is a remarkable film. But know that it’s not a documentary. It is regrettable that it included material that, while honest, earned it an R rating. Eighth Grade is a fictional narrative that is so steeped in truth it’s painful to watch. It possesses an honesty so stark as to be discomforting. That is how good it is. To be 13 is to live with an abiding sense of anxiety and uncertainty, feelings colliding with the need for affirmation, for acceptance, all of which, in the aggregate, are achingly elusive. As Kayla demonstrates in scene after scene (the film is a series of vignettes of her days in class and at home), to be a tweenteen is to experience change, both physically and emotionally. So direct and yet nuanced is this film, so authentic and even quietly harrowing, that the emotions Kayla experiences permeate every frame and are transferred to the audience. Her interactions can seem both conflicted and comical. In one scene, Kayla’s dad, Mark (Josh Hamilton), is driving her to the mall to meet some kids. Nose in her phone, pauses and glances over at her dad and rolls her eyes, saying to him, “Do you have to stare straight ahead like that?” Mark, ever resilient, but a bit of a helicopter parent, wanting above all to make contact with his daughter, patiently answers, “I’m just staring at the road ahead.” Kayla responds, saying, “Well, can you do it another way?” Supremely contraindicated, Kayla posts installments on YouTube wherein she takes on the persona of a life coach, giving advice to anyone out there in the social media ether who might be listening. In one post, looking directly into the computer’s camera, she says, “A big part of confidence is being brave, and you can’t be brave without being scared.” In truth, she understands in spades the scared part (she’s voted the quietest girl in her class, her default setting). What is aspirational for Kayla is the brave part, as she conducts her youthful quest for that geography known as “cool” and “popular.” The contradiction is that her desire to be “fun” is in conflict with her wish to be, at times, anonymous – to just disappear, such as when she’s invited to a popular girl’s house for a pool-birthday party. Her mantra is “Be brave,” yet while standing behind a glass sliding door, dressed in a swimsuit, looking out at a patio-pool filled with kids, she wishes she were anywhere else. What is at the center of Eighth Grade is Kayla’s abiding self-consciousness. She so much wants a social life, a best friend, a boyfriend; yet, feeling the absence of even one kindred spirit she retreats to social media, her only refuge. In the words of coach Kayla, “Life is putting yourself out there – but where is ‘there’?” What she doesn’t realize is that her peers are also clueless about the whereabouts of “there,” no matter how confident they may appear. Eighth Grade. Directed by Bo Burnham. Starring Elsie Fisher, Daniel Zolghadin, Imani Lewis. 1 hr., 33 min. Rated R. Released 2018. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/MAX/Apple tv. What to know about HSAs and FSAs Paying for health care can be challenging – but are you taking full advantage of all the resources available to you? You might have access to a Health Savings Account (HSA) or a Flexible Spending Account (FSA), so let’s look at both. Health Savings Account (HSA) An HSA is a personal savings account used to pay health care costs. If you’re enrolled in a high-deductible health plan, you also may be eligible to contribute to an HSA. You aren’t taxed on the money you put into this account or on the earnings generated from your contributions, as long as withdrawals are used for qualified health care costs such as deductibles, copayments and coinsurance. And there’s no “use it or lose it” provision with HSAs – the money stays in your account until you use it. In fact, you can carry your HSA with you all the way until retirement, when you can use the money to pay for qualified expenses that Medicare or Medicare Supplement Insurance (Medigap) doesn’t cover. In 2023, you can contribute up to $3,850 to an HSA, or $4,850 if you’re 55 or older; for family coverage, you can put in up to $7,750. It’s important to keep in mind that your HSA’s tax benefits only apply when your withdrawals are used for qualified heath care costs. If you use the money for non-qualified expenses, it is considered taxable income, and you may also face a penalty of 20% on the amount withdrawn. However, once you turn 65, you can use your HSA funds for any purpose without a penalty, though the withdrawals will still count as taxable income. Flexible Spending Account (FSA) Now, let’s turn to the Flexible Savings Account. An FSA may be available to you if you get health insurance through your employer. And because you fund your FSA with pretax dollars, your contributions can reduce your taxable income. (In 2023, you can contribute up to $3,050 to an FSA.) Your employer may also choose to contribute to your FSA. Once your account is funded and active, you submit claims with proof of your medical expenses, along with a statement that these expenses aren’t covered by your plan, and you can be reimbursed for your costs. It’s helpful to have a good estimate of your yearly medical expenses for a Flexible Savings Account. That’s because an FSA generally needs to be spent before the end of the plan year – if you don’t use all the money, you can only carry over some of it and any remaining balance is forfeited. (You can carry over up to $610 from 2023 into 2024.) You can’t contribute to an HSA and a traditional FSA in the same year. But if you have an HSA, you might be able to use what’s known as a Limited Purpose Flexible Spending Account (LPFSA) for dental and vision expenses. You’ll need to check with your plan to see if this option is available. Managing your health care expenses should be a key part of your overall financial strategy – so consider putting an HSA or FSA to work for you. articles.text: Raymond Plock passed away in Walnut Creek, California, in late August surrounded by his family. Preceded in death by his wife, Ray is survived by his three children and three grandchildren. Ray lived a full life with family, friends, Boy Scouts and colleagues. He attended high school in Phoenix, Arizona, and worked at his family businesses. After graduating from college he moved to the San Francisco Bay Area, where he worked as a civil engineer for more than 38 years. In years following he was a self-employed consultant. Ray was an avid skier, jogger, backpacker, sailor, and traveler. A mentor to many, he shared his love of the outdoors with his children, grandchildren and Scouting friends. Ray will be greatly missed by all those who knew him. A memorial service is planned for early October. For details, please email: plockfamily@gmail.com. Ray Plock, a resident of Piedmont for many years, passed away in August 2023.

articles.text: Tom Lister, a longtime resident of Piedmont with a laugh that drew everyone closer, passed away on July 1, 2023. Born on November 7, 1934, his family moved to Grosse Pointe, Michigan when Tom’s father was transferred to Detroit by the Santa Fe Railroad. The burglars were wearing hoodies and masks, along with reflective worker vests. The Lexus had a getaway driver who did not leave the vehicle. The license plate on the suspects’ vehicle had been switched so it did not trigger the city’s surveillance camera as a stolen vehicle. (Staff Photo) Senior Fest Continued from page 7 Michael Murphy was called out of retirement to charm the entire class with fun games that had the seniors running around like it was recess. Murphy had the students holding hands and spinning around the infield on Hampton Field then racing to follow his instructions in a scavenger hunt. “Throw your shoes in the middle,” he said as shoes flew through the air. After racing to retrieve their shoes and sit in line Murphy continued, “Okay, now while seated, put your feet in the air.” The food this year was a big hit and students began to line up well before the 11:30 lunch start time as the taco stands were set up by Tacos Jaliscos, filling Hampton Field with the aromas of tacos. The Mr. Softee ice cream truck came by as well, providing a tasty treat on a beautiful late-summer afternoon. Fierce games of Pickleball ensued, as did games of football, basketball, and spikeball. Whether students wanted to sit at the art and crafts table, get a hair braid or race through the inflatable obstacle course, there was something for everyone on Friday.
